lead: Charlotte homes face storm-toppled trees, creek flooding and damp crawl spaces. DryFlare helps owners from Dilworth to Ballantyne get water out and dry quickly.
risk: tree damage in storms, creek flooding and crawl space moisture
risk_short: tree falls, creek floods, crawl spaces
why: Hurricane Hugo reached Charlotte in 1989 and brought down trees across the city, and Helene did the same in 2024. Little Sugar Creek and other creeks flood in heavy rain; after a 1997 flood, the county bought out flood-prone homes and turned land into greenways. Flash floods still hit low streets.

Charlotte grew fast, so most homes are newer, with a median build year of 1995. Newer homes have crawl spaces or slabs and leak mainly from supply lines and appliances. Older homes in Myers Park, Dilworth and Plaza Midwood have plaster walls and older plumbing.
image_alt: Storm damage to a house roof and window
image_caption: Big trees and strong storms often mean roof damage and leaks in Charlotte.
problems: Homes along Little Sugar and Briar creeks
Newer homes in Ballantyne and University City
tips: Have big trees near the house checked before storm season.
Seal the crawl space and run a dehumidifier.
Know where your main water shut-off is.
Check county flood maps before buying near a creek.
areas: Calls come from Uptown, South End, Dilworth, Myers Park, Plaza Midwood, NoDa, Ballantyne and University City, plus Matthews, Huntersville, Concord, Mint Hill and Gastonia.

faq.a: Yes, mainly along creeks like Little Sugar, Briar and McAlpine. The county has bought out many flood-prone homes since the late 1990s. Check flood maps and consider flood insurance if you live near a creek.
